speaker: Vincent Clerc
title: The Potential of Data in Global Trade | Vincent Clerc
question: In global logistics, why do modern economies spend twice as much on transport as on inventory holding compared to the 1980s?
guest: Over the years, we have seen a tremendous improvement in the efficiency of the global logistics system. I have data for the United States: in the 1980s, the US economy would spend more money on inventory holding than on transport within logistics. Today, it spends twice as much on transport than on inventory holding, and this does not mean that transport has become more expensive. Actually, on the contrary, transport has become cheaper. Overall, the long-term trend has been towards more efficient, just-in-time, faster, cheaper transport, which made us buy more of it. Now, there's this saying we have to move from just in time to just in case, which does not mean that we do not need to be as efficient as possible. We need even more reliability, predictability, and port call optimization to arrive when the ship is needed and not to arrive earlier to be more efficient. And at the same time, we need to diversify and shorten supply chains—if it's getting more expensive, some things will no longer be purchased from that far away.

points.core: Transport actually became cheaper over time rather than more expensive.
points.note: Accept: unit shipping/freight costs fell over decades, transport got more cost-efficient rather than pricier. Do not credit: claims that rising fuel, labor, or freight prices drove the higher transport share.

points.core: Cheaper, faster shipping induced companies to buy far more transport volume.
points.note: Accept: lower freight costs and faster transit increased total demand for transport services, Jevons-like volume expansion in shipping. Do not credit: generic statements that global trade grew without linking to lower unit transport costs.

points.core: Firms substituted frequent just-in-time deliveries for expensive warehouse inventory holding.
points.note: Accept: shift to lean/just-in-time supply chains trading lower inventory carrying costs for higher transport spend. Do not credit: vague mentions of supply chain optimization without the transport-for-inventory substitution mechanism.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The premise needs a small correction: economies did not double their transport spending; rather, inventory costs fell much faster than transport costs, so the ratio shifted. The figures below are from memory of US data (the CSCMP State of Logistics reports), not a fresh search, so treat them as approximate.

Around 1980, US inventory carrying costs and transport costs were roughly equal, with total logistics near 16% of GDP. Today logistics is about 8–9% of GDP, and transport is roughly twice the size of inventory carrying.

The main reason is that firms deliberately substituted transport for inventory. Just-in-time and lean practices cut stock levels by relying on smaller, more frequent and faster shipments. Three things made that trade attractive:

- **Deregulation:** US trucking, rail and air reforms around 1980 made transport cheaper and more reliable.
- **Information technology:** barcodes, electronic data interchange, planning software and tracking let information replace safety stock.
- **Interest rates:** rates fell sharply from early-1980s peaks, cutting the cost of financing inventory.

Meanwhile, globalisation and e-commerce lengthened supply chains and added parcel and express delivery, keeping transport demand high.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer: In the early 1980s, inventory holding costs roughly equaled or exceeded transportation spending, driven by double-digit interest rates that made financing stored goods extraordinarily expensive and by rigid, regulated freight markets that required large safety stocks. Over subsequent decades, three structural shifts inverted this balance by systematically substituting movement for storage. First, transport deregulation, containerization, and real-time digital visibility made freight faster and more reliable, enabling just-in-time manufacturing and lean retailing. Rather than warehousing massive buffers, businesses shifted to smaller, more frequent deliveries—a pattern later intensified by rapid e-commerce parcel fulfillment—driving up transport outlays while slashing inventory-to-sales ratios. Second, globalization and offshoring dispersed multi-stage production across continents, vastly lengthening supply chains and multiplying the freight journeys embedded in every finished product. Finally, the long decline in interest rates from their 1980s peak sharply lowered the capital carrying cost of goods still kept on hand, compressing inventory holding expenses even as global freight activity surged.

The response links faster freight to more frequent deliveries and globalization to more freight journeys, but does not link lower freight costs to greater transport demand.
The response explicitly describes firms replacing warehouse buffers with frequent just-in-time deliveries, increasing transport spending while reducing inventory.

noweb.answer: Since the 1980s, modern economies have systematically substituted movement for storage, shifting away from an era when inventory carrying costs nearly equaled transportation spending. In the early 1980s, double-digit interest rates made financing stockpiles extraordinarily expensive, while regulated freight markets kept shipping rigid. Following transportation deregulation and breakthroughs in supply chain software, firms embraced just-in-time manufacturing and lean retailing, deliberately trading large warehouse buffers for smaller, faster, and more frequent shipments. Simultaneously, a multi-decade decline in interest rates sharply lowered the financial cost of holding whatever inventory remained, while barcodes, real-time visibility, and better demand forecasting further shrank safety stocks. Meanwhile, two structural shifts pushed freight spending upward: globalization stretched production across continents, multiplying shipping distances, and e-commerce replaced consolidated bulk retail deliveries with costly, fragmented last-mile parcel fulfillment. Together, cheaper capital, digital inventory precision, globalized sourcing, and rapid delivery expectations compressed holding costs while making continuous, high-velocity transportation the dominant expense in modern logistics.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The premise is roughly right, with one caveat. In the US data (the CSCMP "State of Logistics" reports), total logistics costs fell from about 16% of GDP in 1981 to about 8–9% today. In 1981, inventory carrying costs were about equal to transport costs, or slightly higher. Now transport makes up about 60–65% of logistics spending and inventory about 30%, so roughly two to one. That's a change in the mix, not a rise in transport spending itself.

Four forces explain it. First, the cost of holding inventory fell. Interest rates near 18% in the early 1980s made stock very expensive to keep, and much cheaper capital since then shrank that cost. Second, firms deliberately swapped inventory for transport. Just-in-time and lean production, plus better forecasting and IT visibility, let them keep less stock and ship smaller, more frequent loads. Third, deregulation (the US Motor Carrier and Staggers Acts of 1980) made freight cheaper and more reliable, which made that swap pay off. Fourth, globalization and e-commerce lengthened supply chains and created demand for fast, parcel-level delivery, which pushed transport spending up.

In short, economies now buy speed and frequency in place of buffer stock.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer: Modern economies spend roughly twice as much on transport as on inventory holding not because shipping became more expensive per unit, but because faster, cheaper, and more reliable transport allowed companies to substitute movement for storage. In the early 1980s, high interest rates made capital tied up in stock costly, while slower, less predictable freight forced firms to keep large buffer inventories in warehouses. Over the following decades, deregulation, containerization, and real-time digital tracking dramatically improved freight reliability and lowered unit shipping costs. This enabled just-in-time and lean supply chains, where businesses minimize warehousing expenses by ordering smaller, more frequent, and often faster deliveries. At the same time, globalization and offshoring fragmented manufacturing across continents, stretching supply chains and multiplying the volume and distance of freight in transit. Combined with generally lower interest rates since the 1980s—which directly reduced the financial carrying cost of inventory—these shifts drove inventory holding down while expanding overall demand for transport services.

noweb.answer: Since the 1980s, the balance of logistics spending has shifted heavily from inventory holding to transportation due to a deliberate trade-off between stock and speed, reinforced by macroeconomic and structural changes. First, the widespread adoption of just-in-time manufacturing, lean inventory management, and modern information technology—such as barcoding, enterprise software, and real-time tracking—allowed companies to slash warehouse buffers. Rather than storing large reserves of goods, firms now rely on smaller, more frequent, and faster shipments, effectively substituting transportation for inventory. Second, interest rates in the early 1980s were exceptionally high, inflating the capital cost of holding stock; decades of lower interest rates dramatically reduced inventory carrying expenses relative to freight. Third, globalization and offshoring lengthened supply chains across continents, increasing total shipping distances even as containerization improved efficiency. Finally, the rise of e-commerce shifted retail toward fragmented, high-cost parcel and last-mile delivery, further elevating transport’s share of total logistics expenditure.

points.why: The response credits containerization with improving efficiency but does not establish that unit transport costs fell.
The response attributes longer shipping distances to globalization and more frequent shipments to lean inventory practices without linking increased transport demand to cheaper, faster shipping.
The response explicitly links just-in-time and lean inventory practices to replacing warehouse stock with more frequent shipments.
quotes: the widespread adoption of just-in-time manufacturing, lean inventory management, and modern information technology
firms now rely on smaller, more frequent, and faster shipments, effectively substituting transportation for inventory

In the 1980s, transport and inventory holding accounted for roughly equal shares of logistics costs. Since then, better demand forecasting, real-time inventory tracking, and just-in-time replenishment have let firms hold less stock. That cuts spending on storage and frees up capital that would otherwise be tied up in inventory.

At the same time, global sourcing and production spread across multiple countries have increased the distances that parts and finished goods travel. Leaner inventories also tend to require smaller, more frequent deliveries. Together, these changes explain why transport now accounts for roughly twice the spending on inventory holding. The ratio reflects a shift in how firms manage goods through the supply chain, even where shipping has become cheaper per unit.

The response explains how just-in-time replenishment reduces stock and storage costs while requiring more frequent deliveries.

Since the 1980s, companies have shifted from holding large inventories to replenishing stock more frequently. Better demand forecasting, real-time inventory tracking, and more reliable delivery made just-in-time production and distribution possible. That reduced the money tied up in stock and the cost of storing it.

At the same time, global sourcing lengthened supply routes, and companies increasingly relied on frequent shipments to keep inventories lean. Transport therefore took up a larger share of logistics spending. The roughly two-to-one ratio reflects both lower inventory holding costs and greater reliance on transport, even where shipping became cheaper per unit.

The response attributes greater transport use to global sourcing and frequent replenishment without linking that increase to cheaper, faster shipping.
The response explicitly links frequent replenishment to leaner inventories and lower holding costs.

The ratio shifted mainly because firms found it cheaper to move goods more frequently and reliably than to keep large stocks on hand. Better forecasting, shipment tracking, and just-in-time replenishment let firms hold fewer days of inventory. That freed up working capital and reduced storage costs and losses from goods becoming obsolete. Lower interest rates than in the early 1980s also reduced the cost of financing the inventory firms still held.

Meanwhile, global sourcing lengthened many supply routes, and smaller, more frequent deliveries could cost more per unit to transport. Together, those changes help explain why transport can account for roughly twice as much logistics spending as inventory holding. The ratio describes a shift in the balance of costs, so it can rise even if freight rates stay flat.
